steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the History section of a Wikipedia article on Apptainer (formerly Singularity), the container platform used in HPC — covering where it started, how it spread, and the later split between Apptainer and Sylabs' SingularityCE.

  - started 2015 as open-source project Singularity

- Developer community
  - end of 2016: developers from other research facilities join the LBNL team
- Adoption

  - NIH: Biowulf, 95,000+ core / 30 PB Linux cluster

  - April 2017: on 60% of Open Science Grid network
- Recognition / user base

  - 2017: first place, "Best HPC Programming Tool or Technology"
  - voluntary public registry: >25,000 installations
  - users: Ohio State University, Michigan State University; HPC centers Texas Advanced Computing Center, San Diego Supercomputer Center, Oak Ridge National Laboratory
- Sylabs
  - February 2018: Sylabs announced, founded by Singularity author, commercial support
  - October 2018: version 3.0.0, rewrite in Go
### Apptainer / Singularity split
- May 2020: Kurtzer leaves Sylabs, keeps leadership of open source project
- May 2021: Sylabs forks the project -> SingularityCE
- November 2021: open source project joins Linux Foundation, renamed Apptainer

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Apptainer started out in 2015 as an open-source project called Singularity. A team of researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory led by Gregory Kurtzer developed the first version, which was written in the C programming language, and it was released under the BSD license.

By the end of 2016, many developers from other research facilities had joined the team at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory to work on developing Singularity further.

Singularity very quickly got the attention of scientific institutions around the world that do a lot of computing:

The Stanford University Research Computing Center deployed Singularity on their XStream and Sherlock clusters

The National Institutes of Health installed Singularity on their Linux cluster Biowulf, which has 95,000+ cores and 30 PB

Various sites of the Open Science Grid Consortium, including Fermilab, started adopting Singularity. By April 2017 Singularity was deployed on 60% of the Open Science Grid network.

- HPCwire editors, 2016 and 2017: "One of five new technologies to watch"
- 2017: first place, "Best HPC Programming Tool or Technology"
- voluntary public registry: >25,000 installations; Ohio State, Michigan State; TACC, San Diego Supercomputer Center, Oak Ridge National Laboratory
- February 2018: Sylabs announced, founded by Singularity author, commercial support
- October 2018: version 3.0.0, rewrite in Go

### Apptainer / Singularity split
- May 2020: Kurtzer leaves Sylabs, keeps leadership of open source project
- May 2021: Sylabs fork -> SingularityCE
- November 2021: joins Linux Foundation, renamed Apptainer

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Apptainer started out in 2015 as an open-source project called Singularity. A team of researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory led by Gregory Kurtzer developed the first version, which was written in the C programming language, and it was released under the BSD license.

By the end of 2016, many developers from other research facilities had joined the team at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory to work on developing Singularity further.

Singularity very quickly got the attention of scientific institutions around the world that do a lot of computing:

The Stanford University Research Computing Center deployed Singularity on their XStream and Sherlock clusters

The National Institutes of Health installed Singularity on their Linux cluster Biowulf, which has 95,000+ cores and 30 PB

Various sites of the Open Science Grid Consortium, including Fermilab, started adopting Singularity. By April 2017 Singularity was deployed on 60% of the Open Science Grid network.

In both 2016 and 2017, Singularity was recognized by the editors of HPCwire as "One of five new technologies to watch".

In 2017 Singularity also won first place in the category "Best HPC Programming Tool or Technology".

Based on data entered voluntarily in a public registry, the Singularity user base was estimated at more than 25,000 installations. The users included academic institutions such as Ohio State University and Michigan State University, and also top HPC centers like the Texas Advanced Computing Center, the San Diego Supercomputer Center, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

In February 2018 the Sylabs company was announced, which was founded by the author of Singularity to provide commercial support for Singularity. Then in October of that year Sylabs released version 3.0.0, which was a rewrite of Singularity in the Go programming language.

### Apptainer / Singularity split

In May 2020 Gregory Kurtzer left Sylabs, but he kept the leadership of the Singularity open source project. In May 2021 Sylabs made a fork of the project and called the fork SingularityCE. In November 2021 the Singularity open source project joined the Linux Foundation and it was renamed to Apptainer.

Apptainer started out in 2015 as an open-source project called Singularity. A team of researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory led by Gregory Kurtzer developed the first version, which was written in the C programming language, and it was released[1] under the BSD license.[2]

By the end of 2016, many developers from other research facilities had joined the team at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory to work on developing Singularity further.[3]

Singularity very quickly got the attention of scientific institutions around the world that do a lot of computing:[4]

The Stanford University Research Computing Center deployed Singularity on their XStream[5,6] and Sherlock[7] clusters

The National Institutes of Health installed Singularity on their Linux cluster Biowulf,[8] which has 95,000+ cores and 30 PB[9]

Various sites of the Open Science Grid Consortium, including Fermilab, started adopting Singularity.[10] By April 2017 Singularity was deployed on 60% of the Open Science Grid network.[11]

In both 2016 and 2017, Singularity was recognized by the editors of HPCwire as "One of five new technologies to watch".[12,13]

In 2017 Singularity also won first place in the category "Best HPC Programming Tool or Technology".[13]

Based on data entered voluntarily in a public registry, the Singularity user base was estimated at more than 25,000 installations.[14] The users included academic institutions such as Ohio State University and Michigan State University, and also top HPC centers like the Texas Advanced Computing Center, the San Diego Supercomputer Center, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

In February 2018 the Sylabs[15] company was announced,[16] which was founded by the author of Singularity to provide commercial support for Singularity. Then in October of that year Sylabs released version 3.0.0,[17] which was a rewrite of Singularity in the Go programming language.

### Apptainer / Singularity split

In May 2020 Gregory Kurtzer left Sylabs, but he kept the leadership of the Singularity open source project.[18] In May 2021 Sylabs made a fork of the project[19] and called the fork SingularityCE.[20,21] In November 2021 the Singularity open source project joined the Linux Foundation[22] and it was renamed to Apptainer.[23]

Apptainer began as the open-source project Singularity in 2015, when a team of researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, led by Gregory Kurtzer, developed the initial version, written in the C programming language, and released it[1] under the BSD license.[2]

By the end of 2016, many developers from other research facilities had joined forces with the team at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory to further develop Singularity.[3]

Singularity quickly attracted the attention of computing-heavy scientific institutions around the world:[4]

Stanford University Research Computing Center deployed Singularity on their XStream[5,6] and Sherlock[7] clusters

National Institutes of Health installed Singularity on Biowulf,[8] their 95,000+ core/30 PB Linux cluster[9]

Various sites of the Open Science Grid Consortium, including Fermilab, started adopting Singularity;[10] by April 2017, Singularity was deployed on 60% of the Open Science Grid network.[11]

Two years in a row, in 2016 and 2017, Singularity was recognized by HPCwire editors as "One of five new technologies to watch".[12,13]

In 2017 Singularity also won first place in the category "Best HPC Programming Tool or Technology".[13]

Based on data entered voluntarily in a public registry, the Singularity user base was estimated to be greater than 25,000 installations[14] and included users at academic institutions such as Ohio State University and Michigan State University, as well as top HPC centers like Texas Advanced Computing Center, San Diego Supercomputer Center, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

In February 2018 the Sylabs[15] company, founded by the author of Singularity, was announced [16] to provide commercial support for Singularity. In October of that year Sylabs released version 3.0.0,[17] a rewrite in the Go programming language.

### Apptainer / Singularity split

In May 2020 Gregory Kurtzer left Sylabs but kept leadership of the Singularity open source project.[18] In May 2021 Sylabs forked the project[19] and called it SingularityCE.[20,21] In November 2021 the Singularity open source project joined the Linux Foundation[22] and was renamed Apptainer.[23]
